title: Python
description: Progress through 23 Python lessons from first scripts to typed domain models, reusable CLI tools, resource management, concurrency, profiling and a bounded import pipeline. Three staged projects provide practice and review criteria; completion does not certify professional mastery.
prerequisites: Comfort creating files and opening a terminal; no programming experience required.
A computer with a current supported Python 3 interpreter.
outcomes: Run and explain short Python scripts.
Use values, collections, conditions, loops, and functions to transform data.
Validate inputs, read tracebacks, and persist records as UTF-8 JSON.
Organize modules and understand project environments.
Write small deterministic tests and distinguish API I/O from data processing.
Build and extend a local study log with explicit limitations.
Model invariants with dataclasses; distinguish static contracts from runtime validation.
Build a reusable CLI with cleanup, logging and meaningful failure tests.
Explain threads, async task lifetimes and measurement-based optimization.
Bound external data and preserve prior output on batch or replacement failure.
setup: Install a supported Python 3 release from python.org if needed; this path uses only the standard library.
Confirm python --version (Windows may use py; macOS/Linux may use python3).
Create an empty practice folder. Save each example as a .py file and run it from that folder.
Examples show expected output as comments; the exercise starter and solution are separate snippets. Predict the result, attempt the exercise, then compare the solution.
In lesson 10 create an optional project virtual environment; no third-party packages or live API credentials are required.

Intermediate and advanced practice require Python 3.11+. Download the three project scripts and test_projects.py into one folder, then run python -m unittest -v test_projects.py there. No external packages are required.
nextSteps: Rebuild each stage project from its brief before comparing the reference; explain its failure tests.
Run a separate static type checker and improve contracts; executing annotations does not certify checker coverage.
Package the intermediate tool with pyproject.toml, a build backend and an installed-artifact test in a clean environment.
Use transactional storage when multiple writers or durable service guarantees are required.
Study production API authentication, deadlines, retries, deployment and observability on a real project.
Explore process pools and advanced asyncio cancellation on measured workloads; this path offers advanced practice, not exhaustive mastery.

sources.title: Python tutorial: language and standard-library foundations

lessons.title: 1. Run your first program
lessons.takeaway: A program is a sequence of instructions executed by an interpreter.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Python reads your source code and performs its instructions. A script is a plain text file ending in .py. The interpreter is the program that runs it; a terminal is where you ask the interpreter to run a file.

Save the example as hello.py in a folder you can find. Open a terminal in that folder and run python hello.py. On Windows, py hello.py may work instead; on macOS or Linux the command is often python3 hello.py. Use the same interpreter command throughout this path.

sections.title: Work through an example
paragraphs: print sends a value to the terminal. Quotation marks delimit text, called a string; they do not appear in the output. Python runs these lines from top to bottom.
sections.example:
print("Hello, Python!")
print("One small step")

# Expected output:
# Hello, Python!
# One small step

sections.title: Avoid a common mistake
paragraphs: The interactive prompt shows >>> and runs one instruction at a time. Do not copy >>> into a script. If the terminal cannot find Python, fix the installation or interpreter selection before debugging your code. A file named python.py can also shadow library imports later.

exercise.prompt: Create a greeting script that prints your name on one line and one learning goal on the next. Use the sample values below to check your version.
exercise.starter:
print("YOUR NAME")
# Print your goal next
exercise.solution:
print("Asha")
print("Build a useful script")
checks: Running the script finishes without an error.
There are two lines: Asha, then Build a useful script.
Change both strings and run the file again; the output changes.

quiz.question: What runs the instructions in a .py file?
quiz.explanation: The interpreter executes Python source. The terminal gives you a way to invoke it.

lessons.title: 2. Values, variables, and numbers
lessons.takeaway: Variables name values; arithmetic produces new values.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: An assignment such as count = 3 binds a name to a value. Reading count later retrieves that value. Reassigning count changes what the name refers to; = is assignment, while == compares values.

Integers represent whole numbers, floats represent approximate fractional numbers, strings represent text, and booleans are True or False. Choose names that describe the value, such as minutes_per_day, and use type(value) when you need to inspect a type.

sections.title: Work through an example
paragraphs: The example totals study time and uses an f-string to insert values into text. Division / produces a float. The // operator gives floor division, and % gives a remainder.
sections.example:
minutes_per_day = 25
days = 4
total = minutes_per_day * days
print(f"Total: {total} minutes")
print(f"Hours: {total / 60:.2f}")

# Expected output:
# Total: 100 minutes
# Hours: 1.67

sections.title: Avoid a common mistake
paragraphs: Decimal floats can have tiny representation errors: 0.1 + 0.2 need not equal 0.3 exactly. Avoid exact equality for measured fractional values; for money use integer smallest units or learn decimal.Decimal. A name is case sensitive: Minutes and minutes are different names.

exercise.prompt: Compute the cost of 3 notebooks at 125 cents each. Print total cents and a two-decimal price in dollars.
exercise.starter:
quantity = 3
unit_cents = 125
# Compute and print total
exercise.solution:
quantity = 3
unit_cents = 125
total_cents = quantity * unit_cents
print(total_cents)
print(f"${total_cents / 100:.2f}")
checks: Output is 375 then $3.75.
Changing quantity to 0 yields 0 and $0.00.
The stored total uses integer cents.

quiz.question: What does total = total + 1 do?
options: Binds total to its previous value plus 1
Creates a second variable with the same name
quiz.explanation: The right side is evaluated first, then the name on the left is assigned the resulting value.

lessons.title: 3. Text and user input
lessons.takeaway: Convert text deliberately before doing numeric work.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Strings are sequences of characters. Indexing starts at zero: name[0] is the first character. A slice such as name[:3] selects a portion. len(name) counts characters, and methods such as strip and lower return transformed strings.

input displays an optional prompt and returns a string, even when a user types digits. int converts suitable text to an integer; float converts suitable text to a floating-point number. This lesson uses fixed input text so the example runs without waiting for a person.

sections.title: Work through an example
paragraphs: Trimming surrounding spaces and normalizing case helps compare user input. The example converts the age before adding one. Try replacing raw_age with input("Age: ") after you understand the deterministic version.
sections.example:
raw_name = "  Mira  "
raw_age = "20"
name = raw_name.strip()
age = int(raw_age)
print(f"Hi {name}, next year you will be {age + 1}.")
print(name.lower())

# Expected output:
# Hi Mira, next year you will be 21.
# mira

sections.title: Avoid a common mistake
paragraphs: Strings do not change in place: name.strip() returns a value you must use or assign. int("twenty") raises ValueError; we handle this in lesson 8. Never use eval to interpret user input. Indexing an empty string fails, so inspect length before reading its first character.

exercise.prompt: Normalize the text "  PYTHON  " to lowercase without surrounding spaces, then print its length.
exercise.starter:
raw = "  PYTHON  "
# Normalize and measure
exercise.solution:
raw = "  PYTHON  "
clean = raw.strip().lower()
print(clean)
print(len(clean))
checks: Output is python then 6.
The original raw string still contains spaces.
Replacing raw with "  " yields an empty string and length 0.

quiz.question: What type does input return?
quiz.explanation: Input returns text. Your program decides whether and how to convert it.

lessons.title: 4. Make decisions
lessons.takeaway: Conditions select which instructions run.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A comparison returns a boolean: score >= 50 asks whether the score meets a threshold. An if block runs only when its condition is true. elif tests another condition, and else handles the remaining cases.
Indentation defines the body of a block. Use four spaces consistently. Combine conditions with and, or, and not; use parentheses when the intended grouping is not obvious.

sections.title: Work through an example
paragraphs: The first matching branch wins. Test the highest threshold first here so a score of 85 does not get caught by the lower passing threshold. Predict the output before running.

sections.title: Avoid a common mistake
paragraphs: Use == to compare, not =. Separate conditions such as score >= 50 and score < 80 must each express a comparison; Python also supports 50 <= score < 80. Put boundary values in your checks because > and >= differ at exactly the threshold.

exercise.prompt: Classify a temperature: below 10 is cold, from 10 through 29 is mild, and 30 or above is hot. Start with 30.
exercise.starter:
temperature = 30
# Select a label
checks: 30 prints hot.
10 prints mild; 9 prints cold.
29 prints mild, covering both boundaries.

quiz.question: If both if and elif conditions are true, which branch runs?
quiz.explanation: An if/elif/else chain selects the first condition that is true and skips the remaining branches.

lessons.title: 5. Store related values
lessons.takeaway: Choose a collection by how you need to access and change data.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A list stores an ordered sequence and can be changed with append or item assignment. A tuple is an ordered sequence whose item references cannot be reassigned. A dictionary maps unique keys to values; use meaningful keys for records such as a task title and status.

A set stores unique values and is useful for membership checks and removing duplicates. Set iteration order is not a display contract, so sort a set before producing predictable output. Dictionary indexing raises KeyError for a missing key; get supplies an optional fallback.

sections.title: Work through an example
paragraphs: The list keeps task order, while the dictionary connects task names to durations. A set removes repeated tags. The copy operation matters when you want an independent list instead of another name for the same one.
sections.example:
tasks = ["read", "code"]
tasks.append("review")
minutes = {"read": 15, "code": 30}
print(tasks[1])
print(minutes.get("review", 0))
print(sorted(set(["python", "study", "python"])))

# Expected output:
# code
# 0
# ['python', 'study']

sections.title: Avoid a common mistake
paragraphs: Assigning second = first shares the same list; editing either name edits that list. Use first.copy() for a shallow copy, remembering that nested objects remain shared. {} makes an empty dictionary; set() makes an empty set. List indices start at zero.

exercise.prompt: Create a dictionary for a book with title "Orbit" and pages 120. Increase pages by 10 and print the title and updated pages.
exercise.starter:
book = {"title": "Orbit", "pages": 120}
# Update and print
exercise.solution:
book = {"title": "Orbit", "pages": 120}
book["pages"] += 10
print(book["title"])
print(book["pages"])
checks: Output is Orbit then 130.
The dictionary still has exactly two keys.
A missing optional author can be read with book.get("author", "Unknown").

quiz.question: Which collection maps a task name to its duration?
quiz.explanation: A dictionary stores key/value associations and retrieves a duration using its task-name key.

lessons.title: 6. Repeat work with loops
lessons.takeaway: Loops process each item and accumulate results.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A for loop iterates over items in a sequence or other iterable. range(3) produces 0, 1, and 2; its stop is excluded. An accumulator starts at a neutral value such as 0 and is updated during each iteration.

A while loop repeats while a condition remains true. It is useful when the number of repetitions is unknown, but the body must eventually make the condition false. break exits a loop and continue skips the remainder of the current iteration.

sections.title: Work through an example
paragraphs: This loop includes only study sessions that last at least 20 minutes. The list comprehension expresses the same filtering when a new list is useful. Keep an ordinary loop when there are several actions or complex logic.
sections.example:
sessions = [10, 25, 30]
total = 0
for minutes in sessions:
    if minutes >= 20:
        total += minutes
print(total)
print([m for m in sessions if m >= 20])

# Expected output:
# 55
# [25, 30]

sections.title: Avoid a common mistake
paragraphs: Resetting total inside the loop discards earlier work. Avoid removing list items while iterating over that same list; build a new filtered list. Watch for infinite while loops whose counters never change.

exercise.prompt: Given [2, 5, 8, 11], compute the sum of even numbers with a for loop.
exercise.starter:
numbers = [2, 5, 8, 11]
total = 0
# Add even numbers
checks: Output is 10.
An empty list prints 0.
A list of only odd numbers prints 0.

quiz.question: What values are produced by range(1, 4)?
quiz.explanation: The start is included and the stop is excluded.

lessons.title: 7. Write reusable functions
lessons.takeaway: A function turns inputs into an explicit result.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: def defines a function with parameters: names for its inputs. Calling the function supplies arguments. return sends a result to the caller and ends that call. A function that reaches the end without return produces None.

Variables created inside a function are usually local to that call. Prefer passing data in and returning data out instead of changing global variables. This makes the function easier to reuse and test. A short docstring can explain its contract.

sections.title: Work through an example
paragraphs: The function computes minutes from a number of sessions, and a default argument supplies a usual session length. Printing remains outside the calculation, so another caller could save or compare the returned number.
sections.example:
def study_minutes(sessions, length=25):
    """Return total minutes for equally long sessions."""
    return sessions * length

print(study_minutes(3))
print(study_minutes(2, length=15))

# Expected output:
# 75
# 30

sections.title: Avoid a common mistake
paragraphs: Printing a number does not return it. Avoid mutable defaults such as items=[] because the same list can be reused across calls; use None and create a list inside the function. Name parameters consistently and distinguish a function definition from a function call.

exercise.prompt: Write rectangle_area(width, height) returning the product. Call it for 4 by 3 and for 0 by 7.
exercise.solution:
def rectangle_area(width, height):
    return width * height

print(rectangle_area(4, 3))
print(rectangle_area(0, 7))
checks: Output is 12 then 0.
The function returns a value without printing inside it.
rectangle_area(3, 4) also returns 12.

quiz.question: What is the result of a function with no return statement?
quiz.explanation: Python returns None when execution reaches the end without an explicit return value.

lessons.title: 8. Read errors and validate input
lessons.takeaway: Handle expected failures specifically and let unexpected bugs remain visible.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A syntax error means Python could not parse the program. An exception occurs while a valid program runs, such as converting "abc" to an integer. Read the exception type and message, then find the relevant line in the traceback.

try contains an operation that may fail; except names the failure you know how to handle. raise reports a violated rule. Validation establishes a function contract before the rest of the program uses the data.

sections.title: Work through an example
paragraphs: parse_minutes handles a conversion error and rejects negative values. The caller catches ValueError and gives a useful message. Valid input and invalid input are deliberately tried in the same example.

sections.title: Avoid a common mistake
paragraphs: A bare except can hide programming errors and interrupt signals. Catch a narrow type near the operation you understand. Do not return a fake success value after a failure; the caller should be able to distinguish valid zero minutes from invalid input.

exercise.prompt: Write parse_count(text) that accepts whole numbers of 1 or more and raises ValueError for zero or negative values. Demonstrate "3" and "0".
exercise.starter:
def parse_count(text):
    pass
checks: Output is 3 then count must be positive.
"abc" also raises ValueError from int.
"1" is accepted; do not reject the lower valid boundary.

quiz.question: Which exception should you catch around int("abc")?
quiz.explanation: ValueError describes a value unsuitable for the requested conversion. A narrow handler preserves unrelated failures.

lessons.title: 9. Save files and structured data
lessons.takeaway: Use explicit encoding and JSON to persist ordinary records.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A file stores data after the process ends. pathlib.Path describes a filesystem path. read_text and write_text work with text; specify encoding="utf-8" so behavior is consistent across machines. A relative path is resolved from the current working directory.

JSON represents objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null. json.dumps converts supported Python values to JSON text; json.loads reads JSON text into Python values. Saving and loading are separate operations, and loaded data still needs validation.

sections.title: Work through an example
paragraphs: This example uses a temporary directory so it does not overwrite your own files. It writes a small session record, reads it back, and prints the recovered fields. In your project, choose a deliberate data path.
sections.example:
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
import json

with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    path = Path(folder) / "sessions.json"
    path.write_text(json.dumps({"topic": "loops", "minutes": 25}), encoding="utf-8")
    saved = json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    print(saved["topic"])
    print(saved["minutes"])

# Expected output:
# loops
# 25

sections.title: Avoid a common mistake
paragraphs: Writing a file replaces its previous contents. Do not use a valuable existing file for experiments. JSON object keys become strings, and JSON does not automatically preserve custom classes or tuples. A missing file raises FileNotFoundError and broken JSON raises json.JSONDecodeError; these are different recovery cases.

exercise.prompt: Round-trip a list containing "read" and "code" through a temporary tasks.json file. Print the recovered list length and first item.
exercise.starter:
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
import json
# Write, read, and inspect a list
exercise.solution:
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
import json

with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    path = Path(folder) / "tasks.json"
    path.write_text(json.dumps(["read", "code"]), encoding="utf-8")
    tasks = json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    print(len(tasks))
    print(tasks[0])
checks: Output is 2 then read.
The JSON file contains an array, not Python source.
Repeat with an empty list and verify the length is 0 before indexing.

quiz.question: What does json.loads need as its input?
quiz.explanation: loads parses JSON text; load is the related function that reads from a file-like object.

lessons.title: 10. Modules and project environments
lessons.takeaway: Separate reusable code and select the interpreter intentionally.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A module is a Python file whose definitions can be imported. A package groups modules. Standard library modules ship with Python, while third-party packages require separate installation. Avoid naming your files json.py, unittest.py, or other library names.

A virtual environment gives a project its own interpreter context and installed packages. Create one with python -m venv .venv. On Windows call .venv\Scripts\python.exe directly; on macOS/Linux call .venv/bin/python. Direct invocation avoids shell activation differences. Use that interpreter with -m pip when installing a needed dependency.

sections.title: Work through an example
paragraphs: The runnable example uses only the standard library. For a two-file project, put your function in helpers.py, then import it from main.py in the same folder. The guard if __name__ == "__main__": limits script entry code to direct execution, keeping imports from unexpectedly running the program.

sections.title: Avoid a common mistake
paragraphs: Installing into one interpreter and running another causes confusing missing-module errors. Inspect sys.executable to see which interpreter is active. Keep .venv out of version control and document dependencies; do not copy an environment between machines. No third-party installation is needed for this path.

exercise.prompt: Write format_label(topic, minutes) in helpers.py and import it in main.py. For a quick one-file check, use the solution below; then split the definition and the call into the two files.
exercise.starter:
# helpers.py: define format_label
# main.py: import and call it
checks: One-file output is functions: 20 min.
After splitting files, python main.py gives the same output.
Importing helpers in the interactive prompt does not print anything.
Run the program with the virtual environment interpreter and inspect sys.executable.

quiz.question: Which command ties pip to the selected Python interpreter?
options: Any pip command always selects the right project
quiz.explanation: The -m form runs pip as a module of that interpreter. Substitute your virtual environment interpreter path for python.

lessons.title: 11. Test behavior and understand APIs
lessons.takeaway: Separate data processing from external I/O so it can be checked offline.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A test states an expected behavior for an input. Start with a normal case, an empty case, and an invalid or boundary case. unittest.TestCase supplies assertions and a runner in the standard library; a test failure should identify a behavior worth investigating.

An HTTP API is a remote service accepting requests and returning responses. A response has a status, headers, and body. JSON is one common body format. Networks can time out, services can reject requests, and returned data can differ from what you expected; HTTP success alone does not prove a usable schema.

sections.title: Work through an example
paragraphs: The example processes an API-shaped JSON fixture entirely offline and tests the same parser. Real retrieval could use urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=10) in a with block followed by json.load(response). Keep the URL configured, inspect service documentation, handle HTTPError/URLError, and validate the decoded data before passing it to your calculation.
sections.example:
import json
import unittest

def total_minutes(payload):
    return sum(item["minutes"] for item in payload["sessions"])

class TotalTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_empty(self):
        self.assertEqual(total_minutes({"sessions": []}), 0)

suite = unittest.defaultTestLoader.loadTestsFromTestCase(TotalTests)
result = unittest.TestResult()
suite.run(result)
print(f"Tests passed: {result.wasSuccessful()}")
payload = json.loads('{"sessions":[{"minutes":15},{"minutes":20}]}')
print(total_minutes(payload))

# Expected output:
# Tests passed: True
# 35

sections.title: Avoid a common mistake
paragraphs: A test that only prints a value does not check it. Keep a unit test deterministic: do not depend on a live service staying available. Never place API keys in source or publish them; load credentials from environment variables when a real service needs them. Retrying writes can duplicate actions, so learn the API semantics before retrying.

exercise.prompt: Write count_completed(tasks) for records with a boolean done field. Test an empty list and a list with one completed and one incomplete task. Use unittest assertions, then print the number of passing tests.
exercise.starter:
import unittest
def count_completed(tasks):
    pass
# Add two tests
checks: Output is 2 then True.
Temporarily change the expected mixed result to 2; success becomes False.
Restore the correct expectation after proving the test can fail.
Explain which fields a real API response must provide before this function can use it.

quiz.question: Why use a saved JSON fixture in a unit test?
options: It guarantees the real API never changes
It makes parsing checks deterministic without a network dependency
It removes the need to validate real responses
quiz.explanation: A fixed fixture isolates your parsing behavior. Separate integration checks are needed for a real service.

lessons.title: 12. Capstone: a persistent study log
lessons.takeaway: Combine validation, functions, storage, and checks into a useful small program.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Build a study log that stores records with a topic and nonnegative whole minutes, and reports total minutes. Plan the data format and functions before writing the terminal interface: validate a record, add it to a list, save/load the list, and summarize it.

Keep this first version small. A list of dictionaries is enough; a class is optional, not a requirement. A class would bundle state and methods into objects, useful when behavior grows, but dictionaries and functions make the current contract easy to inspect.

sections.title: Work through an example
paragraphs: The example adds two validated records, saves them in a temporary folder, reloads them, and summarizes the result. The practical exercise extends the program with a topic summary. A real CLI could use argparse for commands such as add and summary; learn that module after the core functions work.
sections.example:
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
import json

def add_session(log, topic, minutes):
    if not isinstance(topic, str) or not topic.strip():
        raise ValueError("topic is required")
    if type(minutes) is not int or minutes < 0:
        raise ValueError("minutes must be a nonnegative integer")
    log.append({"topic": topic.strip(), "minutes": minutes})

with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    log = []
    add_session(log, "Python", 25)
    add_session(log, "Python", 15)
    path = Path(folder) / "study.json"
    path.write_text(json.dumps(log, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
    restored = json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    print(f"Sessions: {len(restored)}")
    print(f"Minutes: {sum(s['minutes'] for s in restored)}")

# Expected output:
# Sessions: 2
# Minutes: 40

sections.title: Avoid a common mistake
paragraphs: Do not silently overwrite malformed data with an empty log. Report JSON or schema errors and keep the file for recovery. Concurrent writers and interrupted writes require more careful storage; this beginner version is for one local process. Before using a permanent file, back it up and add tests for invalid records.

exercise.prompt: Extend the log with totals_by_topic(log), returning a dictionary of accumulated minutes per topic. Use Python 25, Reading 10, and Python 15 as the sample. Then integrate it with lesson 9 storage and lesson 11 tests.
checks: Output is {'Python': 40, 'Reading': 10}.
An empty log returns {}.
Two records with the same topic add instead of replacing the earlier minutes.
Save and reload the sample log; totals stay the same.
Add tests proving blank topics, negative minutes, and True as minutes are rejected by add_session.
Explain an intentional limitation: one process, local file storage, no account system.

quiz.question: What should happen when an existing log contains malformed JSON?
options: Report the error and preserve the file for recovery
Treat it as a successful empty log
quiz.explanation: A parse failure does not mean the user has no data. Preserve the file and make the failure visible.

lessons.title: 13. Classes, invariants and dataclasses
lessons.takeaway: A class groups data and its rules; each instance carries its own state. Methods receive the instance as self. Use a class when this relationship helps explain behavior, rather than wrapping unrelated functions.

sections.title: Reason about the design
paragraphs: A class groups data and its rules; each instance carries its own state. Methods receive the instance as self. Use a class when this relationship helps explain behavior, rather than wrapping unrelated functions.

A dataclass generates construction, representation and equality from annotated fields. It does not enforce annotated types. __post_init__ can enforce invariants after construction; frozen=True blocks ordinary assignment but is not deep immutability.

sections.title: Trace and run
paragraphs: Session is a value object with a nonnegative integer rule. The exact type check rejects booleans because bool subclasses int. hours is derived so it cannot drift away from minutes. Observe equality between independently constructed values.

sections.title: Pitfalls and tradeoffs
paragraphs: Mutable defaults need field(default_factory=list) to create a new list per instance. Prefer composition until inheritance has a clear substitutability contract.
Equality compares fields; it is not persistent identity. Equal topic/duration records can still represent separate events.

exercise.prompt: Build a Playlist dataclass with an independent tracks list and add method rejecting blank titles. Prove two instances do not share state.
exercise.starter: # Implement the contract and edge-case checks.
checks: Run the solution assertions; each checks a behavior, not only printed output.
Change a relevant implementation rule and confirm its check fails, then restore the code.
Explain the normal case, boundary and failure policy in your own words.

quiz.question: Does @dataclass enforce int annotations at runtime?
quiz.explanation: The generated constructor stores values without validating annotated types.

lessons.title: 14. Type contracts and protocols
lessons.takeaway: Annotations express intended inputs and outputs to readers and static checkers. Python execution normally does not enforce them. A checker is a separate tool; this lesson runs without installing one.

sections.title: Reason about the design
paragraphs: Annotations express intended inputs and outputs to readers and static checkers. Python execution normally does not enforce them. A checker is a separate tool; this lesson runs without installing one.
A Protocol describes required operations structurally. An object can satisfy it without inheriting from it, letting consumers depend on a small interface instead of a specific disk or network client.

sections.title: Trace and run
paragraphs: summarize accepts anything with records(). MemorySource gives predictable data without I/O. The declared list[int] is a contract, not a JSON validator; external data needs runtime checks before use.

sections.title: Pitfalls and tradeoffs
paragraphs: Casting JSON to a desired type does not validate it. Check container and value types before constructing domain records.
A runtime-checkable Protocol checks attribute presence rather than full signature/value validity. It is a design aid, not a security boundary.

exercise.prompt: Write normalize_minutes(value: object) -> int accepting actual nonnegative integers. Test zero, True, a string and negative input.
exercise.starter: # Implement the contract and edge-case checks.
checks: Run the solution assertions; each checks a behavior, not only printed output.
Change a relevant implementation rule and confirm its check fails, then restore the code.
Explain the normal case, boundary and failure policy in your own words.

quiz.question: Why use a Protocol?
quiz.explanation: A structural contract permits independent implementations and test doubles with compatible operations.

lessons.title: 15. Iterators and lazy pipelines
lessons.takeaway: An iterable supplies an iterator through iter(). next() retrieves values until StopIteration. Lists are reusable iterables; a generator object is typically a one-pass iterator.

sections.title: Reason about the design
paragraphs: An iterable supplies an iterator through iter(). next() retrieves values until StopIteration. Lists are reusable iterables; a generator object is typically a one-pass iterator.

A generator function yields values while preserving local state. Its body starts during iteration, so errors and effects can be delayed. Lazy stages avoid intermediate lists, but list(...) materializes all results.

sections.title: Trace and run
paragraphs: sum consumes the filtered stream, so a later list finds it exhausted. Call the generator function again for a fresh pass. This example makes consumption visible before introducing file streams.
sections.example:
def valid_minutes(values):
    for value in values:
        if value >= 0:
            yield value
stream = valid_minutes([10, -1, 20])
print(sum(stream))
print(list(stream))
print(list(valid_minutes([0, 5])))

# Expected output:
# 30
# []
# [0, 5]

sections.title: Pitfalls and tradeoffs
paragraphs: Generators are not automatically faster; choose streaming for its memory/lifetime properties and measure relevant workloads.
Do not return an iterator over a file you already closed. Iterate within with or let the generator own a with block and close it deliberately on early exit.

exercise.prompt: Implement running_totals(values) yielding cumulative sums; check empty and partially consumed streams.
exercise.starter: # Implement the contract and edge-case checks.
exercise.solution:
def running_totals(values):
    total = 0
    for value in values:
        total += value
        yield total
assert list(running_totals([])) == []
assert list(running_totals([2, 3, -1])) == [2, 5, 4]
g = running_totals([1, 2])
assert next(g) == 1
assert list(g) == [3]
print("generator checks passed")

lessons.title: 16. Resource lifetimes and cleanup
lessons.takeaway: with gives a resource a bounded lifetime and exits whether the body succeeds or raises. Files and temporary directories already implement this protocol.

sections.title: Reason about the design
paragraphs: with gives a resource a bounded lifetime and exits whether the body succeeds or raises. Files and temporary directories already implement this protocol.
contextlib.contextmanager expresses acquisition before yield and cleanup in finally. Yield exactly once. An exception in the body is delivered at yield; do not accidentally suppress it.

sections.title: Trace and run
paragraphs: The trace records cleanup despite failure, then the outer handler sees the original exception. Prefer a native context manager when the resource already provides one.
sections.example:
from contextlib import contextmanager
trace = []
@contextmanager
def resource():
    trace.append("open")
    try:
        yield "handle"
    finally:
        trace.append("close")
try:
    with resource() as handle:
        trace.append(handle)
        raise ValueError("failed")
except ValueError:
    trace.append("caught")
print(trace)

# Expected output:
# ['open', 'handle', 'close', 'caught']

sections.title: Pitfalls and tradeoffs
paragraphs: Catching an exception inside a context manager without reraising can suppress it. Logging alone is not a reason to hide a failure.
Cleanup itself can fail. Prefer existing tested managers and write custom ones when you own a real lifetime rule.

exercise.prompt: Manage a StringIO buffer and prove it closes while preserving an exception raised by its body.
exercise.starter: # Implement the contract and edge-case checks.
exercise.solution:
from contextlib import contextmanager
from io import StringIO
@contextmanager
def buffer():
    stream = StringIO()
    try:
        yield stream
    finally:
        stream.close()
try:
    with buffer() as stream:
        stream.write("data")
        raise ValueError("original")
except ValueError as error:
    assert str(error) == "original"
assert stream.closed
print("cleanup checks passed")

lessons.title: 17. Packages and command interfaces
lessons.takeaway: Keep domain logic importable and argument parsing at a deliberate entry point.

sections.title: Reason about the design
paragraphs: Keep domain logic importable and argument parsing at a deliberate entry point.

A package groups modules under an import name; a distribution is an installable artifact. __init__.py makes a regular package; __main__.py supports python -m package. For distribution, pyproject.toml declares metadata, Python requirements and a build backend. A src layout can prevent accidental imports from the working tree but needs installation or explicit test configuration.

sections.title: Trace and run
paragraphs: argparse parses argument text and provides help/errors. A fixed argument list makes this example repeatable. The downloadable intermediate tool keeps calculation functions separate from main; publishing a wheel is optional later practice.
sections.example:
import argparse
def parser():
    result = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Summarize study time")
    result.add_argument("minutes", type=int, nargs="+")
    return result
args = parser().parse_args(["10", "20"])
print(sum(args.minutes))

# Expected output:
# 30

sections.title: Pitfalls and tradeoffs
paragraphs: int conversion alone accepts negatives. Apply domain constraints after parsing or in a constrained converter; expected errors should return nonzero status.

Importing a module should not parse arguments or write files. Put the entry call beneath the __main__ guard. Pass argument lists to subprocess without shell=True rather than constructing shell commands from input.

exercise.prompt: Parse --topic and --minutes, rejecting negative minutes with ArgumentTypeError. Prove zero is accepted and a negative exits with status 2.
exercise.starter: # Implement the contract and edge-case checks.
exercise.solution:
import argparse
from contextlib import redirect_stderr
from io import StringIO
def nonnegative(text):
    value = int(text)
    if value < 0:
        raise argparse.ArgumentTypeError("must be nonnegative")
    return value
p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
p.add_argument("--topic", required=True)
p.add_argument("--minutes", required=True, type=nonnegative)
args = p.parse_args(["--topic", "Python", "--minutes", "0"])
assert (args.topic, args.minutes) == ("Python", 0)
with redirect_stderr(StringIO()):
    try:
        p.parse_args(["--topic", "Python", "--minutes", "-1"])
    except SystemExit as error:
        assert error.code == 2
    else:
        raise AssertionError("negative accepted")
print("CLI checks passed")

lessons.title: 18. Logging and test design
lessons.takeaway: Test contracts and failure behavior, then log useful operational facts.

sections.title: Reason about the design
paragraphs: Test contracts and failure behavior, then log useful operational facts.

Use normal cases, boundaries and invariants such as save/load preservation. Temporary fixtures isolate tests from personal files. unittest supports assertRaises, assertLogs and subTest for diagnosed failure cases. Logs explain operations; they do not replace return values or assertions.

sections.title: Trace and run
paragraphs: A dedicated logger and StringIO handler make this warning deterministic. Applications choose handlers and levels; reusable modules should not globally configure logging. The project suite combines real temporary storage with one mock of the replacement boundary.
sections.example:
import logging
from io import StringIO
stream = StringIO()
logger = logging.getLogger("lesson.validation")
logger.handlers.clear()
logger.propagate = False
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)
handler = logging.StreamHandler(stream)
handler.setFormatter(logging.Formatter("%(levelname)s:%(message)s"))
logger.addHandler(handler)
logger.warning("rejected record %s", 2)
print(stream.getvalue().strip())
logger.removeHandler(handler)
handler.close()

# Expected output:
# WARNING:rejected record 2

sections.title: Pitfalls and tradeoffs
paragraphs: Avoid secrets and raw sensitive payloads in logs. Include safe identifiers/counts that explain which operation failed.

Tests that only print or mirror a private helper can miss a broken contract. Demonstrate a relevant deliberate defect fails. Patch dependencies where the consumer looks them up, and keep ordinary pure-function tests on real code.

lessons.title: 19. Threads, futures and async tasks
lessons.takeaway: Choose concurrency by workload and keep shared state controlled.

sections.title: Reason about the design
paragraphs: Choose concurrency by workload and keep shared state controlled.

Concurrency overlaps progress; parallelism executes simultaneously. Threads commonly suit blocking I/O. CPU-bound Python often benefits from processes on conventional GIL-enabled builds; free-threaded builds/extensions change tradeoffs. asyncio cooperatively schedules coroutines at await points, and TaskGroup provides bounded task lifetimes and failure propagation.

sections.title: Trace and run
paragraphs: Executor.map returns results in input order even if completion order differs. The caller aggregates returned values rather than workers changing shared totals. This tiny calculation demonstrates mechanics, not a speedup. The exercise uses simulated async I/O without any service.
sections.example:
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
def score(value):
    return value * value
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) as pool:
    results = list(pool.map(score, [3, 1, 2]))
print(results)
print(sum(results))

# Expected output:
# [9, 1, 4]
# 14

sections.title: Pitfalls and tradeoffs
paragraphs: A future.result timeout limits waiting; it does not terminate a running thread. Executor context exit normally waits for work, so real blocking operations need their own deadlines.

Blocking code inside a coroutine stops event-loop progress. Cancellation is cooperative and must preserve cleanup. Bound tasks and workers; tiny tasks can cost more to schedule than to run. Do not let workers concurrently rewrite one JSON file.

exercise.prompt: Collect two simulated I/O values with asyncio.TaskGroup, retaining task handles so output remains ordered. Run as a script with Python 3.11+.
exercise.starter: # Implement the contract and edge-case checks.
exercise.solution:
import asyncio
async def read_minutes(value):
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    return value
async def collect():
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as group:
        tasks = [group.create_task(read_minutes(v)) for v in [10, 20]]
    return [task.result() for task in tasks]
values = asyncio.run(collect())
assert values == [10, 20] and sum(values) == 30
print("async checks passed")

lessons.title: 20. Profiling and complexity
lessons.takeaway: Check correctness, then measure representative workloads before optimizing.

sections.title: Reason about the design
paragraphs: Check correctness, then measure representative workloads before optimizing.

Big-O describes cost growth, not exact runtime. Repeated rescans can dominate constant-factor changes. cProfile helps locate cumulative time; timeit repeats focused measurements. Report workload size, environment and methodology. tracemalloc tracks Python allocations rather than every native allocation.

sections.title: Trace and run
paragraphs: The aggregation visits each row once. Its profile is inspected but only deterministic data and call-count presence are printed. Actual timings vary; the exercise compares equivalent algorithms without a brittle speed assertion.
sections.example:
import cProfile, pstats
from collections import defaultdict
def totals(rows):
    result = defaultdict(int)
    for topic, minutes in rows:
        result[topic] += minutes
    return dict(result)
profile = cProfile.Profile()
answer = profile.runcall(totals, [("Python", 10), ("Python", 20), ("Reading", 5)])
stats = pstats.Stats(profile)
print(answer)
print(stats.total_calls > 0)

# Expected output:
# {'Python': 30, 'Reading': 5}
# True

sections.title: Pitfalls and tradeoffs
paragraphs: Compare equivalent behavior before timing; a fast incorrect shortcut is not an optimization. Include empty and edge cases.
Decide whether data setup belongs in timed work. Warm caches, build configuration and input distribution matter. Never turn a particular speedup into a universal unit-test expectation.

lessons.title: 21. External input and security boundaries
lessons.takeaway: Parsing, schema validation and authorization are separate steps.

sections.title: Reason about the design
paragraphs: Parsing, schema validation and authorization are separate steps.

JSON decoding establishes syntax, not expected shape. Check exact fields, types, sizes and ranges before constructing domain objects. Bound bytes before parsing, plus record count and field lengths. Never eval user input or deserialize untrusted pickle.

sections.title: Trace and run
paragraphs: The parser limits encoded bytes, requires exact fields and rejects booleans as minutes. Normalization is an explicit policy; a schema-valid record still does not prove its sender has permission. The full project also rejects duplicate JSON keys.

sections.title: Pitfalls and tradeoffs
paragraphs: A size check after reading an entire file does not prevent the allocation. Read at most limit+1 bytes at the real boundary and reject excess.

This local project assumes trusted directories. Path containment alone cannot defeat hostile symlink races; production isolation and authentication require a separate deployment design. Bounded JSON still needs care with deeply nested hostile documents.

lessons.title: 22. Safe replacement and failure recovery
lessons.takeaway: Prepare a complete new file before replacing previous output.

sections.title: Reason about the design
paragraphs: Prepare a complete new file before replacing previous output.

Direct writing truncates an existing file before the new data is complete. A same-directory temporary file lets you write, flush and fsync its contents, close it, then replace the target with os.replace. Atomic visibility differs from power-loss durability and concurrency control.

sections.title: Trace and run
paragraphs: Closing before replacement matters on Windows. finally removes abandoned temporary files after preparation or replacement failure. Validate data before entering the write path. Tests inject a failure at the I/O boundary rather than relying on a real disk fault.
sections.example:
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory, NamedTemporaryFile
import json, os
def replace_json(path, value):
    temporary = None
    try:
        with NamedTemporaryFile("w", encoding="utf-8", dir=path.parent, delete=False) as stream:
            temporary = Path(stream.name)
            json.dump(value, stream)
            stream.flush()
            os.fsync(stream.fileno())
        os.replace(temporary, path)
    finally:
        if temporary is not None and temporary.exists():
            temporary.unlink()
with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    path = Path(folder) / "log.json"
    replace_json(path, [1])
    replace_json(path, [1, 2])
    print(json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")))
    print(len(list(Path(folder).iterdir())))

# Expected output:
# [1, 2]
# 1

sections.title: Pitfalls and tradeoffs
paragraphs: Atomic replacement does not prevent two read-modify-write operations losing updates. Use coordinated ownership, a lock or transactional storage before accepting multiple writers.
Power-loss durability can require directory syncing and platform-specific guarantees. Do not hide malformed files or permission failures by pretending the log is empty.

exercise.prompt: Write save_text and inject os.replace failure. Prove the old bytes survive and the temporary file is cleaned.
exercise.starter: # Implement the contract and failure checks.
exercise.solution:
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory, NamedTemporaryFile
from unittest.mock import patch
import os
def save_text(path, text):
    temporary = None
    try:
        with NamedTemporaryFile("w", encoding="utf-8", dir=path.parent, delete=False) as stream:
            temporary = Path(stream.name)
            stream.write(text)
            stream.flush()
            os.fsync(stream.fileno())
        os.replace(temporary, path)
    finally:
        if temporary is not None and temporary.exists():
            temporary.unlink()
with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    path = Path(folder) / "data.txt"
    path.write_text("old", encoding="utf-8")
    with patch("os.replace", side_effect=OSError("injected")):
        try:
            save_text(path, "new")
        except OSError:
            pass
        else:
            raise AssertionError("failure hidden")
    assert path.read_text(encoding="utf-8") == "old"
    assert list(Path(folder).iterdir()) == [path]
print("replacement failure checks passed")

lessons.title: 23. Capstone: a bounded import pipeline
lessons.takeaway: Validate a complete batch before one deliberate commit.

sections.title: Reason about the design
paragraphs: Validate a complete batch before one deliberate commit.

Build an importer for newline-delimited records with id, topic and minutes. IDs must be unique. Bound input, validate all rows and save a versioned report only when all pass. This policy keeps partial success from looking like a complete import.

sections.title: Trace and run
paragraphs: The mini example shows ordered workers and batch validation. advanced_project.py adds frozen domain records, duplicate JSON-key rejection, limits, logging and same-directory replacement. Run --demo with temporary files, then run test_projects.py before extending it. Threads demonstrate composition, not a promised speed advantage.
sections.example:
import json
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
def parse_line(text):
    value = json.loads(text)
    if type(value) is not dict or set(value) != {"id", "minutes"}:
        raise ValueError("invalid fields")
    if not isinstance(value["id"], str) or not value["id"]:
        raise ValueError("invalid id")
    if type(value["minutes"]) is not int or value["minutes"] < 0:
        raise ValueError("invalid minutes")
    return value
def import_batch(lines):
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) as pool:
        rows = list(pool.map(parse_line, lines))
    if len({row["id"] for row in rows}) != len(rows):
        raise ValueError("duplicate id")
    return rows
rows = import_batch(['{"id":"a","minutes":10}', '{"id":"b","minutes":20}'])
print([r["id"] for r in rows])
print(sum(r["minutes"] for r in rows))

# Expected output:
# ['a', 'b']
# 30

sections.title: Pitfalls and tradeoffs
paragraphs: Do not publish each worker's output as it finishes. Collect and validate the batch, then commit once. A failing worker does not forcefully terminate remaining threads.

The full project assumes one writer and a trusted local directory. It has no account system, network retries, sandbox, database transaction or power-loss certification. State those limits in your project review.

exercise.prompt: Inject a publish callback and prove valid rows publish once while duplicate IDs publish zero times; repeat with the full file importer.
exercise.starter: # Implement the contract and failure checks.
exercise.solution:
def import_and_publish(rows, publish):
    ids = [row["id"] for row in rows]
    if len(set(ids)) != len(ids):
        raise ValueError("duplicate id")
    publish(rows)
calls = []
import_and_publish([{"id": "a"}, {"id": "b"}], calls.append)
assert len(calls) == 1
calls.clear()
try:
    import_and_publish([{"id": "a"}, {"id": "a"}], calls.append)
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("duplicate accepted")
assert calls == []
print("commit policy checks passed")

project.solution:
"""Foundation reference: validated study records and topic totals."""
import json
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

def add_session(log, topic, minutes):
    if not isinstance(topic, str) or not topic.strip():
        raise ValueError("topic required")
    if type(minutes) is not int or minutes < 0:
        raise ValueError("minutes must be a nonnegative integer")
    log.append({"topic": topic.strip(), "minutes": minutes})

def totals_by_topic(log):
    totals = {}
    for row in log:
        totals[row["topic"]] = totals.get(row["topic"], 0) + row["minutes"]
    return totals

def demo():
    log = []
    add_session(log, "Python", 25)
    add_session(log, "Reading", 10)
    add_session(log, "Python", 15)
    with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
        path = Path(folder) / "study.json"
        path.write_text(json.dumps(log), encoding="utf-8")
        restored = json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
        print(totals_by_topic(restored))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    demo()
